title: Hang a dish-rack cutlery caddy on the rack's side rail by its two hooks
instruction: Hang the caddy on the rack's rail by both hooks, and let go.
context: Anyone who washes up by hand has a drainer whose cutlery caddy hooks over the rack's side rail. Once the cutlery is loaded, the caddy is lifted off the counter and hung back on the rack: both hooks must straddle the rail together and the caddy must hang square against the rack's wall. Lowered a few millimetres off, a hook lands on top of the rail and the caddy stands crooked; hooked on one hook only, the first knock drops it with the cutlery in it. The job ends with the hands off, the caddy hanging still and every fork still in it.
setup: Bimanual YAM station; the table top is z 0. x points forward from the line through the two arm bases, y to the left of the midpoint, z up; arm bases at y +305 mm and -305 mm. (1) A fixed rack side wall of plastic-coated steel wire, dark grey, centred on y -110 mm: a top rail, round, 10 mm across, 260 mm long along y (y -240 to +20 mm), its axis at x 330 mm and z 135 mm (top at z 140 mm); two lower wires, round, 6 mm across, 260 mm long, axes at x 328 mm and z 40 and 85 mm; two vertical end posts, round, 6 mm across, 135 mm tall, at y -235 and +15 mm and x 328 mm. The rail and the lower wires share one tangent plane at x 325 mm on the robot's side. (2) Behind the wall, fixed: a light grey polypropylene draining tray, 230 x 300 x 12 mm (x 335 to 565 mm, y -260 to +40 mm), and two white ceramic side plates, 180 mm across and 8 mm thick, standing on edge in the tray with their faces across y at y -155 and -65 mm (x 370 to 550 mm, up to z 192 mm). (3) A loose cutlery caddy, blue polypropylene, 0.062 kg: a slim open box 18 (x) x 76 (y) x 100 (z) mm outside, walls and base 3 mm, with two 2 mm dividers 90 mm tall that make three slots 22 mm wide. It stands on the table with its base down at x 200 mm, y -210 mm (x 191 to 209, y -248 to -172 mm), its back wall (the +x face) toward the rack. The back wall carries two hooks centred 24 mm either side of its middle (y -234 and -186 mm), each 12 mm wide: the wall's own 3 mm tab rises 26 mm above the rim; a 4 mm bridge runs from the tab's top 25 mm toward the rack; a 4 mm rear leg hangs 30 mm below the bridge, 18 mm clear of the tab (the rail is 10 mm), its last 12 mm bent 42 degrees outward as a lead-in. Hung with both bridges resting on the rail, the back wall leans on the lower wires and the base is 14 mm above the table. (4) Three loose forks, 0.04 kg each, steel grey: 120 mm long, handle 12 mm wide, head 16 mm wide, three 3 mm tines, all 8 mm thick. One stands upright in each slot, tines on the caddy's floor, handle up, with its middle at x 200 mm, z 63 mm and y -234, -210 and -186 mm: tines on the floor's top (z 3 mm), top at z 123 mm, 23 mm above the rim, 2 mm clear of the front and back walls and 3 mm of the dividers. Nothing else is on the table. Real build: a slim dish-rack cutlery caddy with two hook clips (the common drainer type, hooks gapped about 18 mm over a 10 mm rail), or print one in PETG: box 76 x 18 x 100 mm, 3 mm walls and base, two 2 mm dividers, two 12 mm wide hooks as above; rack: any wire drainer with a 10 mm round side rail, or a 10 mm rod on posts. Forks: any three small steel forks (cake or child's, 120 to 140 mm, 2 to 3 mm thick); they lean in a slot and that is fine.
scoring: End state, read at the last step from the poses of the caddy and the forks and from both grippers. Seated (per hook): the rail's axis, taken at the hook's centre line and read in the caddy's frame, lies in the hook's gap (the rail's surface no more than 1 mm inside either leg's inner face), the bridge's underside is from 2 mm below to 3 mm above the rail's top, the hook's centre is at least 12 mm inside the rail's ends, and the caddy faces the rack and stands upright (yaw and tilt each within 30 degrees; hung on the far side, turned away or upside down, no hook is seated). Hung: both hooks seated, the caddy's yaw within 5 degrees of the wall's normal and its tilt within 5 degrees. Cutlery kept: all three forks' middles over the caddy's footprint, above its floor and below its rim. Hands off: on every step of the last 1 s both grippers' finger zones are 30 mm or more from the caddy and the forks, and over that 1 s the caddy moves under 5 mm and turns under 5 degrees (visibly motionless). Score 0 if at any time the caddy's or a fork's middle falls more than 50 mm below the table top (off the table), and 0 unless hands off. Otherwise: 1.0 hung, cutlery kept; 0.5 hung with a fork out of the caddy; 0.25 one hook seated (hooked on one hook only), or both seated with the caddy crooked (yaw or tilt over 5 degrees); 0 otherwise, including a caddy on the table, or hanging with a leg or bridge perched on top of the rail. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0. Success: 1.0 held for 1 s. In a real trial, per condition: seated, a 3 mm feeler under each bridge, a look from above for the rail between the legs (a 1 mm feeler between rail and each leg) and a rule for the hook's distance from the rail's end (12 mm); yaw and tilt, a 5 degree angle gauge against the back wall and a spirit-level card; cutlery kept, a look from above; hands off, a 30 mm spacer against each hand and 30 fps video of the last 1 s with a ruler and a printed 5 degree wedge beside the caddy (it must not visibly shift or swing); fall, a rule.
fidelity: Rigid bodies. Hook gap 18 mm on a 10 mm rail (4 mm slack a side, with a lead-in tip; real hooks 1 to 3 mm). The caddy is slim (18 mm deep) and the sim forks are 120 mm slabs 8 mm thick so they stand in 12 mm gaps; real forks are 2 to 3 mm and lean, which the scoring allows (a fork only has to stay in). Friction 0.35 plastic on coated wire, 0.30 steel on plastic (est). No software rules.
reset_notes: Stand the caddy on the table, base down, at x 200 mm, y -210 mm, its back wall (the hooks) toward +x. Stand one fork upright in each slot, tines down, handle up (middles at y -234, -210, -186 mm). Nothing is consumed; the rack, tray and plates stay put.
